A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Shot2Story research work, despite renaming and substantial revision. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original captioning, summarization, retrieval, and zero-shot question-answering experiments, plus prompt-sensitivity results and qualitative analyses in its supplement.

after.justification: v3 reports original captioning, summarization, external question-answering, and new Shot2Story-QA results, with additional qualitative evidence in its appendices.

M1.justification: v3 replaces separate visual and narration prediction targets with their concatenation, adds VideoChat2/UMT-L captioning and summarization variants with LoRA, and specifies updating both Q-Former and MLP for MiniGPT4. The two-stage SUM-text pipeline is removed. The core shot-structured summarization and summary-to-Vicuna QA procedures remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluated Shot2Story-QA tasks covering temporal, holistic, and audio-related understanding. It combines visual and narration captioning into a joint task and removes text-to-video, text-to-shot, and video-to-text retrieval. MSRVTT-QA and ActivityNet-QA remain; the larger HD-VILA sample alone does not establish new domain coverage.

E2.justification: VAST becomes an evaluated captioning baseline, while VideoChat2, LLaMA-VID, and Video-LLaVA enter the experimental comparisons. VALOR's narration comparison and the Alpro, CLIP4clip, and UMT retrieval comparisons disappear. The separate Video-ChatGPT summary-based QA comparator in v1 Table 6 is also removed.

E3.justification: Reported training videos increase from 14,016 to 36,951, captioning epochs change from 40 to 10, summarization batch size from 16 to 32, and caption generation limits from 150 to 180 tokens. v3 adds 90,000 GPT-V-labeled summarization training videos. Its new QA protocol includes length and model-based filtering, 4,905 validation and 6,465 test pairs, and category-averaged accuracy; the original video validation/test counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The two-stage versus end-to-end summarization comparison and four-prompt sensitivity study in v1 Table 7 are removed. v3 adds raw-audio controls for VAST, an ASR-input comparison for Video-ChatGPT, and Shot2Story-QA failure cases examining action order and audiovisual correspondence. Shot-structure and ASR analyses remain but are revised for the new models and targets.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Dataset distributions and annotation-correction percentages are descriptive results rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Captioning and summarization results are extensively replaced: SUM-shot's CIDEr of 8.6 in v1 Table 4 becomes 7.6 for MiniGPT4-SUM-shot in v3 Table 3 under changed training conditions. New Shot2Story-QA overall scores are 32.5 and 40.5 for the two proposed variants. MovieChat's reported MSRVTT-QA/ActivityNet-QA scores change from 49.7/51.5 to 52.7/45.7. Retrieval and prompt-sensitivity result tables disappear.

T1.justification: Both versions are empirical benchmark papers without a formal theoretical development. No substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are added or removed.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion now present a dedicated multi-shot QA benchmark as a central contribution. Retrieval drops from the declared task suite, and separate captioning tasks become joint captioning. The central claim that detailed summaries support video understanding remains, while the abstract changes its performance-boost assertion to competitive performance.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning human-centric selection bias, omitted minor details, and emphasis on salient objects. It attributes QA weaknesses to missing audio inputs and multi-shot training, discusses action-order and cross-shot identity failures, and adds a single-shot generalization interpretation. Earlier explanations favoring two-stage SUM-text and retrieval alignment are removed.

D1.justification: v3 documents QA-generation prompts and filtering, GPT-V generation with Whisper-X speaker diarization, and VAST training resources, while removing SUM-text implementation details. Appendix E changes from requiring source-video downloads to stating that cropped videos are provided and maintained; a repository link replaces the project-page pointer. Documentation remains imperfect: Appendix D's VAST modalities conflict with Table 2.

R1.justification: The existing dataset comparisons largely remain. v3 adds focused positioning against existing QA benchmarks and citations for VideoChat2/MVBench, LLaMA-VID, Video-LLaVA, LoRA, and Zhang et al., while removing retrieval-related references and VALOR. It also acknowledges prior frame-caption-based video QA, narrowing v1's assertion that such work had not been done for videos.

P1.justification: The experiment narrative is substantially rewritten and consolidated around joint captioning, summarization, and separate external and in-domain QA discussions. Separate narration and retrieval sections disappear, while annotation and appendix explanations are expanded and reorganized. Dataset/model terminology, author information, and cross-references are revised throughout.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format. Comparison tables are redesigned around modalities and training data; new QA-distribution, annotation, GPT-V, and qualitative QA displays are added. The single-shot architecture diagram and retrieval/prompt-sensitivity tables are removed, while several retained figures are relocated or revised.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important gap in v1 by directly testing temporal, holistic, and audio-related multi-shot understanding through human-checked Shot2Story-QA, rather than relying principally on caption overlap and external QA. Broader model comparisons, explicit annotation-bias discussion, and the stated cropped-video release substantially improve benchmark utility and transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of retrieval, SUM-text, and prompt-sensitivity evidence, although comparator-based question filtering and appendix inconsistencies—including the stale 8.6 CIDEr statement in Appendix C.2—limit interpretation and reproducibility.
